analysis.one_liner: Extends subsidized ACA marketplace premiums to households earning above the current income cutoff.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 36 Democratic cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, only households earning up to four times the poverty line can get premium tax credits to buy marketplace health insurance, and even subsidized households pay part of their premium out of pocket. This bill would remove the income cutoff entirely, so households above the limit could buy subsidized coverage, and would lower the out-of-pocket premium share at every income level (for example, the top subsidized share falls from 9.96% to 8.5% of income). It would take effect in 2026 and apply permanently. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning above four times the poverty line who buy their own health insurance instead of getting it through an employer — a group that today gets no subsidy at all no matter how expensive their premiums are. It also lowers premium costs for everyone already receiving subsidies, roughly two-thirds of whom have no employer coverage options. Health insurers gain millions of new subsidized customers. [S2]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Self-purchasing households above the subsidy cutoff

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 400%-of-poverty income ceiling on premium tax credits, so middle-income households facing full unsubsidized marketplace premiums become eligible for the first time.
Caps out-of-pocket premiums at 8.5% of income for households above 400% of poverty, instead of the current cliff where they can pay unlimited premiums.
Reduces premium shares for everyone below the cutoff — the top subsidized percentage drops from roughly 9.96% of income to 8.5%.
Strikes the affordability provisions that blocked workers from claiming the credit when employer coverage was deemed affordable, widening access further.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a permanent expansion of a refundable tax credit — the Congressional Budget Office treats such expansions as large, ongoing federal spending. Higher-income marketplace customers also benefit, since the credit would apply with no income cap, so a share of the new cost goes to subsidizing relatively well-off households. [S2]

drawbacks.text: The expanded credit would apply to households at every income level with no ceiling above 400% of poverty, meaning substantial federal subsidies would flow to relatively high earners, not just to families of modest means.
Making the expansion permanent rather than temporary commits future Congresses to open-ended spending; temporary extensions are the form Congress has historically been willing to pass.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly addresses a real affordability cliff: a modest raise can push a self-employed worker over 400% of poverty and from subsidized coverage into paying $15,000+ a year for family premiums. The design is less targeted than it could be — no income cap means some subsidies reach households that don't need them — and the permanent cost is significant. On balance it is a straightforward affordability expansion whose main objections are fiscal rather than structural.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and later to its Health Subcommittee, and the Republican-run committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood introduced the bill on September 24, 2024, with 35 Democratic cosponsors including senior members like Steny Hoyer and Frank Pallone.
All 35 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill went to the House Ways and Means Committee, which was controlled by Republicans in the 118th Congress.

On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee — a routine step — and there were no hearings, markups, or floor actions before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households already just above the subsidy cutoff keep paying full premium price, and the federal Treasury keeps the money it would have spent. No committee chair or faction lost anything by letting the bill expire.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: Treasury, and no one else in particular

for.name: Rep. Lauren Underwood
for.role: Sponsor, Health Care Affordability Act of 2024
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 35 Democratic cosponsors, including senior members Steny Hoyer and Frank Pallone.

for.name: 35 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill in the three-plus months before the Congress ended; it sat at subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: Removing the income cutoff and lowering premium shares creates millions of new subsidized customers for marketplace insurers, and caps what enrollees pay, making coverage more affordable. The public benefit and the insurers' gain run in the same direction here, though it also entrenches the existing system where subsidies flow through private insurers rather than a public plan.
